source.title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease
source.authors: Tamoghna Chattopadhyay; Kartik Shelar; S. Thomopoulos; Paul M. Thompson

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. There are minor formatting and typesetting artifacts, but the text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a data-scaling framework in a new setting—3D MRI disease classifiers—and reports measured performance as training-set size changes.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocations. Its power-law eigenvalue-spectrum measurements are representation geometry, not loss-scaling results. It cites language-model scaling laws and reports its own MRI-classifier AUROC scaling results; cited results are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study cites Kaplan et al. only as background. Its own results concern how a classifier's AUROC changes with the number of labelled MRI scans (N) for small (3–6M parameter) or frozen encoders. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, and fits no power law to AUROC versus N. It also does not relate downstream performance to pretraining scale or loss. Training-set-size curves for a disease classifier are a related but different construct, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude three further points. The spectral geometry (the rank-1 spike) is a property of the trained encoder rather than the classification contrast, shown by the frozen-encoder 2×2 design; the clean separation holds only for MINiT. The collapse arises in the transformer, not the ABMIL pooling. Measuring the spike on a pilot sample can indicate whether more data will help.
record.recipe_differences: The paper applies spectral and Zeta Law analyses to 3D MRI classification and AUROC versus sample size, rather than measuring language-model cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome differs by encoder and classification contrast: DINO AUROC rises with N, the supervised Dementia-vs-CN curves are described as flat, and the MCI-vs-CN probes remain near chance. The paper also reports that the forward model overpredicts in the near-chance regime.

fits_no_version.finding: In 3D MRI disease classification, AUROC versus labelled training size N rises for frozen DINO (0.683 at N=50 to 0.793 at N=2822). It stays flat for supervised ViT3D, MINiT and NIT encoders on Dementia vs CN, and stays near chance (0.51–0.53) on MCI vs CN. The Zeta Law forward model overpredicts by 0.12–0.23 on MCI vs CN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Classifier sample-size scaling (AUROC versus labelled N) depends on the encoder's learned representation: collapsed supervised encoders plateau, while non-collapsed self-supervised encoders keep improving.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised encoders show a detached PC1 spike above a power-law bulk spectrum: S=11.4–25.6 on Dementia vs CN and 3.4–9.4 on MCI vs CN. DINO shows no spike (S=0.66). A RESET test finds curvature in the bulk spectrum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised training of MRI transformers produces a rank-1 spike in the embedding spectrum that tracks with the encoder, not the task contrast.

record.problems: The study uses one dataset (ADNI) and two binary tasks. MCI/CN performance is near chance, and the authors report that threshold estimates are unstable there and that the forward model overpredicts. DINO was pretrained on ImageNet, with a possible domain gap noted by the authors. The study does not test language-model loss scaling.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional spectral quantities, frozen-encoder threshold comparisons, and pooling-ablation results in Tables 2–6 and Figures 1–6. They were left out where they do not measure the versions of the claim about language-model loss scaling or downstream performance as a function of scale.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute: not measured.
Extrapolating small runs to larger runs: not tested.
Effect of architecture shape at fixed parameter count on loss: not tested.
No loss power law in the MRI modality or under fine-tuning; only AUROC versus labelled N, with no power-law fit.
Downstream performance versus pretraining scale or loss: not measured.
Dependence of exponents on fitting choices: not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link is wrong. V6 concerns downstream performance as a function of pretraining scale or loss, whereas this study's N is the number of labelled scans used to train the classifier. The study is not one of the original sources; it is a bioRxiv preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count on language-model loss.
The version concerns the same power-law form for loss across modalities and training regimes. This study measures MRI-classifier AUROC and embedding spectra, not loss scaling in those regimes.

Tests AUROC versus training-sample size for MRI classifiers only; does not test language-model downstream tasks, parameter or compute scaling, or downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation on parameter counting, schedules, data, and fitting choices.

rows.subject: DINO

rows.operation_detail: Measured observed AUROC as the training-set size varied
rows.note: The paper reports these as endpoint values of a rising observed curve.
rows.check: This is DINO linear-probe AUROC versus the probe's training-set size N, not downstream performance versus pretraining scale or loss. It bears on no version, so V6 is wrong.

rows.subject: Three supervised encoders: ViT3D, MINiT, and NIT (reported together)
rows.operation_detail: Measured observed AUROC as the training-set size varied; the paper reports the three encoders together as staying flat
rows.value: Stayed flat across the reported range; exact values not stated
rows.note: The study states the aggregate result for the three supervised encoders rather than giving separate numeric curves in the text.
rows.check: This shows flat AUROC versus classifier training N for supervised encoders; no values are given in the text. It is not pretraining scale or loss, so V6 is wrong.

rows.subject: Linear probes across the 12 frozen-encoder cells (reported together)
rows.operation_detail: Swept training-set size and evaluated linear-probe AUROC on a fixed test set
rows.note: The paper reports the near-chance outcome across all 12 cells in aggregate.
rows.check: Near-chance probe AUROC versus N on MCI/CN is classifier sample-size scaling, not a scaling-law version.

rows.subject: Zeta Law forward model applied to the MCI/CN frozen-encoder cells (reported together)
rows.operation_detail: Compared predicted AUROC curves with observed MCI/CN performance across training-set sizes
rows.measure: Predicted AUROC and discrepancy from observed AUROC
rows.baseline: Observed AUROC stayed near chance at all N
rows.value: Predicted AUROC 0.69–0.93; overshot observed AUROC by 0.12–0.23
rows.uncertainty: Estimated bias in squared Mahalanobis distance was 0.042–0.069; 1–15% of measured squared distance
rows.note: The paper says removing the estimated bias barely changed the fit: RMSE 0.176 to 0.169.
rows.check: This compares the paper's own Zeta Law forward-model prediction with observed AUROC. It is the study's method evaluation, not a test of a version, and should not be a V6 row.
